title: The Son who works on the Sabbath
sum: At a festival in Jerusalem, Jesus walks among the sick at the pool of Bethesda and picks out a man who has been ill for thirty-eight years. The man does not ask for help and shows no faith; he only explains that someone always beats him into the stirred water. Jesus tells him to stand up, lift his mat and walk, and he does. But it is a Sabbath, and carrying a mat is work. The authorities challenge the man, he points them to Jesus, and the conflict that runs through the rest of John begins.

Jesus's defense is short and startling: "My Father is at work right up to now, and I am at work too" (5:17). His hearers understand it as a claim to share God's own work, which no Sabbath stops, and so to be equal to God. The long speech that follows (5:19–47) explains what kind of equality he means. The Son does nothing on his own; he does what the Father does: he gives life and he judges. Then, like a defendant in court, Jesus calls his witnesses: John the Baptist, his own works, the Father, the Scriptures, and finally Moses, whom his accusers trust, but who, he says, wrote about him.
readings: From 5:16 on, the chapter is a court scene. Jesus is accused of breaking the Sabbath and of blasphemy. He answers the charge (5:17–30) and then produces witnesses, as the Law required (5:31–47; Deuteronomy 19:15). By the end the roles have reversed: the accused becomes the judge to whom the Father has given all judgment, and Moses, the accusers' champion, is called as a witness against them.
Read as a story about two kinds of response

The healed man never believes in Jesus as far as we are told, and he reports him to the authorities. Chapter 9 tells a mirror story: another healing on a Sabbath, with a pool, a man questioned by the authorities, Jesus finding him afterward, but this time a man who comes to faith and is thrown out for it. Literary critics such as R. Alan Culpepper and Jeffrey Staley have drawn out the pairing. Read side by side, the two chapters show that a miracle does not by itself create faith, and that the key to the healed man may be 5:40: "you are not willing to come to me."
Read as a sermon on the Sabbath

Jewish teachers asked how God rests on the Sabbath while the world goes on. Jesus answers within that debate: God never stops giving life and judging, and the Son shares that work. The healing on the Sabbath is not careless law-breaking; it is a sign of the Sabbath's purpose, God's life-giving rest, now arriving.

views.H: John's detail about Bethesda, by the Sheep Gate with five porches, was once taken as symbolism. Excavations at St. Anne's Church found two pools divided by a dam, which most scholars think had porticoes on four sides and across the middle, though some (Gibson) dispute the middle one. The unnamed festival leaves the chronology open; if it was a Passover, John's account covers more than three years.
views.C: Many scholars notice that chapter 6 fits better right after chapter 4 (Jesus in Galilee, then crossing the lake) and that 7:1 follows naturally from 5:18 (he stayed out of Judea because the Jews wanted to kill him). Some, such as Rudolf Bultmann, rearranged the chapters. Others think John's order is deliberate, or that the Gospel grew in stages. The shift between present eternal life (5:24–25) and future resurrection (5:28–29) is another place where scholars see layers, or a deliberate both-and.
views.L: The chapter turns a healing into a discourse, as John often does: sign, controversy, speech. Key words return: "work," "life," "judgment," "testimony." The speech moves from the Son's relation to the Father (5:19–30) to the witnesses to the Son (5:31–47), and it ends with questions, not a response from the hearers.
views.J: "The Jews" here are the Jerusalem authorities, who enforce Sabbath law in the Temple. The argument is an inner-Jewish one about the Sabbath, about God's work, and about how to read Moses. Jewish scholars note that the charge "equal to God" (5:18) reflects later conflicts between the synagogue and John's community, and that John's harsh picture of "the Jews" was used against Jews for centuries. Others, like Daniel Boyarin, argue that a second divine figure beside God was thinkable within Judaism at the time.
views.T: The fathers of the church read 5:17–30 as a key text for the doctrine of the Trinity: the Son is equal to the Father in power and honor (5:23) and yet receives everything from him (5:19, 26). Augustine's sermons on John explore "the Father has life within himself" and gave it to the Son as the eternal begetting. Many read the pool allegorically: the five porches as the Law of Moses, which shows sickness but cannot heal; the stirred water as baptism.

deep.h: The pool of Bethesda: what was found
deep.b:
In the 1800s and 1900s excavations beside the Crusader church of St. Anne, north of the Temple Mount, uncovered a large double pool cut into the rock, about 100 meters long, divided by a rock wall or dam, together with pieces of columns. The pools probably began as reservoirs in the time of the high priests (perhaps 200s BC), and Josephus calls the district north of the Temple Bezetha. East of the pools were small baths, caves and channels.

Most scholars, following Joachim Jeremias's The Rediscovery of Bethesda (1966), reconstruct colonnades on all four sides and along the dam, which would give John's five porches. That reconstruction is debated. Shimon Gibson has argued that the southern pool was a large stepped pool for ritual bathing and questioned whether a portico ever stood on the dam. Urban von Wahlde defends the view that the site fits John's description. Either way, two pools of the right size stood where John puts them.

After the Romans rebuilt Jerusalem as Aelia Capitolina (after AD 135), the site held a healing shrine of Asclepius and Serapis, with offerings shaped like healed body parts. Whether a healing cult existed there before AD 70 is debated, but John 5:3 and 5:7 suggest that the sick gathered there expecting to be cured. Christians later built a Byzantine church over the site, and the Crusaders another.

deep.h: Why did Jesus heal on the Sabbath?
deep.b:
Jesus did not need to heal this man on a Sabbath; he had been ill for thirty-eight years and could have waited a day. He also told him to carry his mat, which by the rules of the time was forbidden work. So the Sabbath is not an accident in the story. In all four Gospels Jesus heals on the Sabbath on purpose (Mark 3:1–6; Luke 13:10–17; 14:1–6; John 9:14).

In the Synoptic Gospels Jesus defends this from the Law's purpose: it is lawful to do good on the Sabbath, and the Sabbath was made for people (Mark 2:27; 3:4). In John the argument is different and bolder. God himself does not stop giving life and judging on the Sabbath (5:17), and Jesus does the same work. The Sabbath, which looked back to God's rest after creation, is now the day on which God's new work of giving life is shown.

Christians have drawn different conclusions. Most churches teach that Jesus fulfilled the Sabbath and that Christians gather on Sunday, the day of his resurrection. Seventh-day Adventists and Seventh Day Baptists keep Saturday and read Jesus's Sabbath healings as freeing the day from human rules, not abolishing it. See the topic page on the Sabbath.

At the end of chapter 4 Jesus is in Cana of Galilee. Chapter 5 takes him to Jerusalem. Then 6:1 says he went "across the Sea of Galilee," as if he had been in Galilee all along. And 7:1 says he stayed in Galilee because the Jews in Judea wanted to kill him, which follows 5:18 well. Because of this, some scholars, including Rudolf Bultmann and others before him, suggested that chapters 5 and 6 were accidentally switched or that the Gospel was edited in stages.

No manuscript has the chapters in another order. Many scholars therefore read the present order as John's own: he arranges his story around the festivals (Sabbath in chapter 5, Passover in 6, Booths in 7) more than around travel. Chapter 5's claim that Moses wrote about Jesus (5:46) is also the bridge to chapter 6, where Jesus is compared with Moses and the manna.

echoes: Genesis 2:2–3; Exodus 20:8–11; Jeremiah 17:21–22; Nehemiah 3:1; Nehemiah 13:15–19; Deuteronomy 2:14; Deuteronomy 4:12; Deuteronomy 18:15–18; Deuteronomy 19:15; Deuteronomy 31:26; Deuteronomy 32:39; 1 Samuel 2:6; Daniel 7:13–14; Daniel 12:2; Psalm 132:17; Mark 2:1–12; Mark 3:1–6; 9:1–41; 10:30–33; 1 John 5:9–12

settings.what: Jesus and the man at the pool
settings.to: One sick man lying at Bethesda, alone and without anyone to help him
settings.when: at the pool during a festival Sabbath (5:6–8), and later when Jesus found him in the Temple (5:14)
settings.why: To offer healing to a man who had not asked for it, then to warn him afterward that something worse than illness, judgment, lay ahead if he went on sinning. The words were meant to move him from a cure to a changed life; the story does not say whether they did.
settings.readers: For John's readers the scene showed that Jesus's gifts come first and freely, and that being healed is not the same as believing (5:40).
views: Some read 5:14 as a sign that this man's illness came from a particular sin.
Others read "something worse" as final judgment (5:29), and note that in 9:3 Jesus denies that suffering always comes from sin.

settings.to: "The Jews": the Temple authorities in Jerusalem who were pursuing him
settings.when: on a festival Sabbath, after they learned that he had healed a man and told him to carry his mat
settings.why: To answer the charge of Sabbath-breaking, not by arguing about the rules but by pointing to God, who keeps giving life and judging even on the Sabbath. The hearers were experts in Sabbath law and probably knew the debate about whether God rests; they understood at once that Jesus was claiming to share God's work (5:18).
settings.readers: For John's first readers, late in the first century, the scene explained why Jesus was rejected by the leaders in Jerusalem, and why the church claimed that Jesus does the works of God.

settings.what: The Son's defense: life, judgment and four witnesses
settings.to: The same Jerusalem authorities, who were seeking to kill him for making himself equal to God
settings.why: To explain the claim of 5:17. The Son is not a rival god; he does nothing on his own (5:19, 30). But the Father has given him the two works that belong to God alone, giving life and judging (5:21–27), so honoring the Son is honoring the Father (5:23). Then, because one witness is not enough under the Law (Deuteronomy 19:15), Jesus calls John, his works, the Father, and the Scriptures, and ends by turning Moses, his hearers' hope, into their accuser. The speech was meant to show learned hearers that their own Scriptures point to him, and to warn them that rejecting him is rejecting the God they want to honor.
settings.readers: Many scholars think that for the Gospel's readers, many of whom had been in conflict with synagogue leaders, the speech gave the church's answer to the charge that Christians worship two gods: the Son is equal in honor because he shares the Father's work, and he receives all things from the Father.
views: Traditional readers take 5:19–47 as Jesus's words on this occasion, given in John's own style.
Many critical scholars see it as a composition by the evangelist or his community, drawing on sayings of Jesus and shaped by later debates with the synagogue (J. Louis Martyn).

traditions.q: If the believer "is not coming into judgment" (5:24), how can all be judged by what they did (5:29), and can a believer be sure of eternal life now?
views: Eternal life begins in baptism and grace, and the last judgment will reveal the works that grace has produced, so faith and works are judged together. Without a special revelation no one can know with the certainty of faith that he will persevere to the end, though Christians may have firm hope.

Salvation is a journey of union with God (theosis). The believer already shares divine life, yet must keep faith and repentance to the end; the Orthodox avoid claims of final certainty and pray for mercy at the dread judgment seat of Christ.

The believer is justified by faith alone and can be certain of salvation because it rests on God's promise, not on works. The deeds named in 5:29 are the fruits of faith that show it is living, but faith can be lost through unbelief.

Those who believe have passed from death to life and will never come into condemnation; true believers will persevere. At the last judgment their works are shown as the evidence of grace, not the ground of acceptance, and believers may attain full assurance.
Believers can know they are children of God by the witness of the Spirit, but they can fall away by turning from God, so final salvation depends on continuing in faith that works by love.

Most Baptists teach that all true believers endure to the end and cannot finally fall away, so 5:24 gives present assurance; 5:29 describes the good works that flow from saving faith. Some Free Will Baptists hold that a believer can fall away.

title: Bread from heaven
sum: Near Passover, on the hills across the Sea of Galilee, Jesus feeds a crowd of about five thousand men with a boy's five barley loaves and two small fish, and the leftovers fill twelve baskets. The crowd sees the Prophet like Moses and wants to make Jesus king by force, so he withdraws. That night the disciples row into a storm and see Jesus walking on the sea. He says, "I am. Stop being afraid," and the boat at once reaches the shore.

Next day the crowd finds him in Capernaum, and the bread of life discourse begins (6:26–59). Asked for a sign like the manna, Jesus says the Father now gives the true bread from heaven, and then: "I am the bread of life" (6:35). Whoever comes to him and believes will never hunger. When the listeners complain like Israel in the wilderness, he speaks of being drawn by the Father, and then, more shockingly, of eating his flesh and drinking his blood. Many disciples leave. Jesus asks the Twelve whether they will go too, and Peter answers for them: "Lord, who would we go to? You have the sayings of eternal life" (6:68).
readings: The chapter retells Israel's escape from Egypt in order: Passover (6:4), a crowd fed in the wilderness, a crossing of the sea where God walks on the waters, bread from heaven, complaining, and a test of loyalty. Jesus takes the place of Moses and, more than that, of the God who gave the manna. Peder Borgen argued that 6:31–58 follows the pattern of a Jewish sermon on the text "Bread from heaven he gave them to eat."

The thanksgiving over bread (6:11, 23), the Passover setting, and the words about eating flesh and drinking blood (6:51–58) lead many readers, from the early church to the present, to hear the Eucharist. John has no institution of the Supper at his Last Supper (chapter 13); on this reading, chapter 6 is where he teaches what the Supper means.
Read as a call to faith

Others stress that eternal life is promised to whoever believes (6:35, 40, 47) in the same words later used for eating and drinking (6:54). On this reading, "eating" is believing in the Jesus who gives his flesh in death for the world, and the chapter is about receiving him, not about a rite. Many scholars hold the two readings together.

views.H: The feeding is the only miracle of Jesus in all four Gospels (Matthew 14:13–21; Mark 6:30–44; Luke 9:10–17). John's own details (barley loaves, a boy, Philip and Andrew, the attempt to make Jesus king) fit Galilee in the first century, where popular leaders were sometimes proclaimed king. The second Passover (6:4) is part of John's longer timeline. Excavations at Capernaum show a synagogue from about AD 400 built over an older basalt building.
views.C: John's sequence (feeding, sea crossing, demand for a sign, discourse on bread, Peter's confession) matches Mark 6–8 closely, so scholars debate whether John knew Mark or drew on a parallel tradition (C. H. Dodd argued for independent tradition). Some critics, following Bultmann, think 6:51c–58 is a sacramental addition by a later editor; most now read the discourse as a unity built on the manna text.
views.L: The chapter is built on misunderstanding: the crowd wants bread, Jesus offers himself. The first "I am" saying with a picture comes here (6:35). Key words repeat: "bread," "from heaven," "come down," "give," "eat," "life," "the last day." The audience shrinks scene by scene: five thousand, the crowd in Capernaum, "the Jews," many disciples, the Twelve, and one devil among them.
views.J: The discourse is a Jewish argument about a Jewish text, the manna, given at Passover in a synagogue (6:59). The hope that the Messiah would bring back the manna was real (2 Baruch 29:8). The "Jews" who complain (6:41, 52) are Galileans who know Jesus's family. The words about drinking blood would have shocked any Torah-observant listener (Leviticus 17:10–14), and John does not soften that.
views.T: From Ignatius and Irenaeus onward, many fathers read 6:51–58 of the Eucharist, and the Catholic and Orthodox churches read it in their liturgies of Holy Communion. Augustine taught that to believe is to eat, and also that the sacrament is received rightly only by faith and love. At the Reformation, 6:63 ("the flesh is of no use") became a battle text between Zwingli and Luther. The chapter is also central to the debates about grace and free will (6:37, 44, 65).

deep.b:
Peder Borgen's study Bread from Heaven (1965) compared John 6:31–58 with Jewish sermons in Philo and the later midrash. These sermons quote a text, then explain it word by word, and end by returning to the opening words. John 6 does exactly that with "Bread from heaven he gave them to eat" (6:31):

  • "He gave": not Moses, but my Father gives (6:32).
  • "Bread from heaven": the bread of God comes down from heaven and gives life (6:33–51).
  • "To eat": whoever eats this bread will live forever (6:49–58).

The closing line, "Here is the bread that came down out of heaven... Anyone who eats this bread will live forever" (6:58), sums up the text. Seeing the pattern helps explain why the discourse moves from believing (6:35–47) to eating (6:51–58): it is working through the words of its text.

deep.h: Does John 6 teach the Lord's Supper?
deep.b:
Three positions have long histories.

  • Yes, directly. The Catechism of the Catholic Church reads 6:51–58 as Jesus's promise of the Eucharist. The Council of Trent based the real presence mainly on the words of institution, and used John 6 in its teaching on Communion while noting that the fathers interpreted the chapter in more than one way. Orthodox and many Anglican and Lutheran readers also hear the Eucharist here. They point to the Passover setting, "gave thanks" (6:11, 23), the move from "believe" to "eat and drink," the strong verb in 6:54, and "my flesh is true food" (6:55).
  • No, it is about faith. Luther himself said in 1520 that John 6 does not speak of the sacrament but of faith in the incarnate Word, though he firmly held the real presence on other grounds. Calvin said the discourse is not about the Supper, but about the feeding by faith that the Supper seals. Zwingli used 6:63 against any bodily eating. Many Baptist and evangelical readers say eating is believing (6:35, 47).
  • Both, at two levels. Many modern scholars, Catholic and Protestant (Raymond Brown among them), see a discourse about faith in the crucified Jesus that John's readers would also have heard as speaking about their Supper.

See the card below for how each church answers.

Three verses in this chapter set God's action beside human coming: "Everything the Father gives me will come to me" (6:37), "Nobody is able to come to me unless the Father who sent me draws him" (6:44), and "unless the Father has given it to him" (6:65). Yet the chapter also says "anyone who comes to me I will never throw out" (6:37), and blames the hearers for not believing (6:36, 64).

Augustine, preaching on 6:44, said the Father draws not by forcing the will but by delight, as you draw a sheep by showing it a green branch. Calvin read these verses as teaching that God's drawing is effective in all whom he chooses. Arminius and Wesley read them with 12:32, where Jesus says he will draw all people to himself: God's drawing goes to everyone and enables them to come, but it can be resisted. The verse is one of the classic battlegrounds of the debate on grace and free will; see the card below.

echoes: Exodus 12; Exodus 16; Numbers 11; Deuteronomy 8:3; Deuteronomy 18:15–18; 2 Kings 4:42–44; Psalm 77:19; Psalm 78:24–25; Psalm 107:23–30; Job 9:8; Proverbs 9:5; Isaiah 54:13; Isaiah 55:1–3; Leviticus 17:10–14; Matthew 14:13–33; Matthew 16:13–23; Mark 6:30–52; Mark 8:11–33; Luke 9:10–20; 1 Corinthians 10:1–4; 1 Corinthians 10:16–17; 1 Corinthians 11:23–26; Revelation 2:17

settings.to: Philip, then Andrew and the disciples
settings.when: on the mountain near Passover, as a large crowd came toward them
settings.why: To test Philip (6:6): would he see only the arithmetic of what money could buy, or look to Jesus? The question echoes Moses' cry in the wilderness about feeding the people (Numbers 11:13), and prepares the disciples to see who is feeding the crowd.

settings.to: The disciples in the boat, rowing at night against a strong wind
settings.when: far out on the lake, after the feeding, as they saw him walking on the sea
settings.why: To calm their terror by making himself known. The words identify him ("It's me") and, on the waters where only God walks, also echo God's own "I am" in Isaiah. They were meant to turn fear into recognition.
settings.readers: For later readers facing storms of persecution, the scene promised that Jesus comes to his disciples in the dark.

settings.to: The crowd he had fed, who crossed the lake to find him; later "the Jews" of Capernaum who complained (6:41, 52); spoken in the synagogue at Capernaum (6:59)
settings.when: the day after the feeding, near Passover, when the crowd came looking for more bread and asked for a sign like Moses' manna
settings.why: To lift the hearers from the bread they had eaten to the giver. They wanted a Moses who would feed them every day; Jesus tells them God is now giving the true bread from heaven, himself, and calls them to come and believe. When they complain, he tells them that coming is the Father's gift, and then presses the offense further: his flesh, given in death, must be eaten and his blood drunk. Knowing that the hearers were Galilean Jews at Passover, steeped in the manna story and the food laws, explains both their hope and their shock.
settings.readers: For John's first readers, the discourse answered questions in their churches: why many Jews, and some disciples, had left; what it means to receive Jesus; and what their own meal of bread and cup meant.
views: A synagogue sermon on the manna
Borgen and others read it as a homily on Psalm 78:24 and Exodus 16, given in the synagogue setting John names.
Many critical scholars think John built the discourse from sayings of Jesus and early Christian preaching, some adding that 6:51–58 was added in a later edition with the Eucharist in view.

settings.to: First the wider circle of disciples who were complaining, then the Twelve
settings.when: right after the synagogue discourse, as many disciples found the teaching too hard and began to leave
settings.why: To face his followers with the offense of his words and let them choose. He points beyond the cross to his going up (6:62), says that life comes from the Spirit through his words (6:63), and gives the Twelve the freedom to go. Peter's answer shows the purpose: not that they understood everything, but that they knew there was nowhere else to find eternal life. The warning about a "devil" (6:70) tells them that even the chosen circle is not safe from betrayal.
settings.readers: For later readers who had seen friends leave the faith, the scene shows that falling away happened in Jesus's own circle, and gives Peter's words as the answer of those who stay.

traditions.q: Is eating Jesus's flesh and drinking his blood (6:53–58) about the Lord's Supper, and how is Christ received?
views: Yes. Jesus promises the Eucharist, in which bread and wine become his true body and blood (transubstantiation). The Catechism reads 6:51–58 this way; the Council of Trent grounded the real presence in the words of institution and used John 6 in its teaching on Communion, noting that the fathers read the chapter in more than one way. "The flesh is of no use" (6:63) means a merely human, fleshly understanding.

Yes. In the Divine Liturgy the faithful receive the true body and blood of Christ for the forgiveness of sins and eternal life, as John Chrysostom preached on this chapter. The Orthodox affirm the change of the gifts as a mystery without defining it in philosophical terms.

Christ's body and blood are truly present in, with and under the bread and wine and are received by mouth by all who commune. But Luther taught that John 6 speaks directly of spiritual eating by faith, not of the sacrament, which rests on the words of institution.

John 6 describes the feeding on Christ by faith through the Spirit, which happens apart from the Supper too; the Supper seals it. In the Supper believers truly but spiritually feed on Christ's body and blood, received by faith, not bodily present in the elements.

The Thirty-Nine Articles teach that Christ's body is given, taken and eaten in the Supper only in a heavenly and spiritual manner, received by faith, and they reject transubstantiation. Anglicans are divided: Anglo-Catholics hold a strong real presence and read John 6 sacramentally; evangelicals read it of faith.
Wesley's Articles follow the Anglican teaching: a real, spiritual presence received by faith, not a change of substance. Methodists call the Supper a means of grace and invite all who seek Christ.

Eating and drinking in John 6 means believing in Christ (6:35, 47). The Lord's Supper is an ordinance of remembrance in which believers spiritually feed on Christ by faith (1689) or simply memorialize his death (Baptist Faith and Message). Zwingli's reading of 6:63 is often cited.

traditions.q: When Jesus says no one can come "unless the Father ... draws him" (6:44, 65), can that drawing be resisted?
views: No for the elect: God gives a definite people to the Son (6:37, 39) and effectually draws them, renewing their wills so that they come freely and surely. All whom the Father draws, Christ raises on the last day (6:44).

Human beings cannot come to Christ by their own powers; conversion is entirely God's work through Word and Sacrament. Yet the grace God offers to all can be resisted, and those who are lost are lost by their own fault, not by God's choice.
No one comes without God's prior grace, which draws by delight and not by force (Augustine). The human will, moved by grace, freely cooperates and can also refuse; God wills all to be saved.
Salvation is synergy: God draws and enables, and the person freely responds. God's grace goes before, but it never overrides human freedom.
God's prevenient grace draws every person, as Jesus promises to draw all people (12:32), restoring enough freedom to respond. That drawing can be resisted, and those who resist are responsible.
Divided. Calvinistic Baptists (1689 Confession) teach effectual calling; many Southern and General Baptists hold that God's drawing is consistent with human free agency and can be refused.
